b2-politikairetorika-01.title: Communicative Challenge: The Heroes' Square Statues
b2-politikairetorika-01.scenario: At Heroes' Square in Budapest, a visiting student asks you why the statues in the colonnade were changed after the Second World War.
b2-politikairetorika-01.prompt: Tell her why the monument was built, and say which statues replaced the Habsburg rulers.
cues: Say who decided to build it
Name the figures who replaced the Habsburgs
b2-politikairetorika-01.target: A dualista korszak vezetői arra a döntésre jutottak, hogy a honfoglalás ezeréves évfordulójára emlékművet emelnek. A második világháború után a Habsburg uralkodók helyére Bocskai István, Bethlen Gábor, Thököly Imre, II. Rákóczi Ferenc és Kossuth Lajos szobra került.
b2-politikairetorika-01.english: The leaders of the Dualist era reached the decision to erect a monument for the thousandth anniversary of the Conquest. After the Second World War, statues of István Bocskai, Gábor Bethlen, Imre Thököly, Ferenc Rákóczi II and Lajos Kossuth replaced the Habsburg rulers.
b2-politikairetorika-01.canDo: I can explain the historical design and political symbolism of the Millennium Monument at Hősök tere.

b2-politikairetorika-02.title: Communicative Challenge: The Avenue With Many Names
b2-politikairetorika-02.scenario: On a walk along Andrássy út, a visiting student asks you what the avenue was called under the Rákosi regime and what the people of Budapest did with the official names.
b2-politikairetorika-02.prompt: Tell her why the avenue was renamed under Rákosi and what happened to the name of the Oktogon in everyday speech.
cues: Say whose name the avenue received and why
Say what people said in everyday speech
b2-politikairetorika-02.target: A pártvezetés abban a szellemben döntött az átnevezésről, hogy az út a szovjet vezető nevét viselje. A budapestiek a hétköznapi beszédben azonban továbbra is az Oktogont használták.
b2-politikairetorika-02.english: The party leadership decided on the renaming in the spirit that the avenue should bear the name of the Soviet leader. However, the people of Budapest went on using the name Oktogon in everyday speech.
b2-politikairetorika-02.canDo: I can explain how Budapest street names served as ideological palimpsests across 20th-century political regime changes.

b2-politikairetorika-03.title: Communicative Challenge: Memento Park
b2-politikairetorika-03.scenario: At Memento Park, a visiting student asks you why the communist-era statues of Budapest were not simply destroyed.
b2-politikairetorika-03.prompt: Tell her what Budapest's leaders proposed and what the architect wanted the park to be.
cues: Say what the city's leaders proposed
Say what the architect wanted the park to be
b2-politikairetorika-03.target: Budapest vezetése azzal a kezdeményezéssel állt elő, hogy a szobrokat ne olvasszák be. Eleőd Ákos azzal a céllal tervezte a parkot, hogy mementó legyen.
b2-politikairetorika-03.english: Budapest's leadership came forward with the initiative that the statues should not be melted down. Ákos Eleőd designed the park with the aim that it be a memento.
b2-politikairetorika-03.canDo: I can describe the concept and cultural significance of Ákos Eleőd's Memento Park (Szoborpark).

b2-politikairetorika-04.title: Communicative Challenge: Two Orators
b2-politikairetorika-04.scenario: In the Parliament building in Budapest, a visiting student asks you how the speeches of Deák and Kossuth differed.
b2-politikairetorika-04.prompt: Tell her what Deák proceeded from and what Kossuth was known for.
b2-politikairetorika-04.target: Deák Ferenc abból a megfontolásból indult ki, hogy a törvényesség tisztelete hozhat tartós sikert. Kossuth ezzel szemben a romantikus pátosz mestere volt.
b2-politikairetorika-04.english: Ferenc Deák proceeded from the consideration that respect for legality could bring lasting success. Kossuth, by contrast, was a master of romantic pathos.
b2-politikairetorika-04.canDo: I can analyze the historical rhetorical styles of great Hungarian parliamentary orators (Kölcsey, Deák, Kossuth, Apponyi).

b2-politikairetorika-05.title: Communicative Challenge: Memory Politics
b2-politikairetorika-05.scenario: On Szabadság tér in Budapest, a visiting student asks you what memory politics means and why the monuments on the square are debated.
b2-politikairetorika-05.prompt: Tell her what Bibó István warned about and what question memory politics is about.
cues: Say what question memory politics is about
b2-politikairetorika-05.target: Bibó István arra figyelmeztetett, hogy az állandó félelem politikai hisztériához vezethet. Az emlékezetpolitika arról a kérdésről szól, hogy ki értelmezi a múltat.
b2-politikairetorika-05.english: István Bibó warned that constant fear can lead to political hysteria. Memory politics is about the question of who interprets the past.
b2-politikairetorika-05.canDo: I can analyze the politics of memory (emlékezetpolitika) in Central Europe and explain István Bibó's diagnosis of collective historical hysteria.

b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.title: Communicative Challenge: Monuments and Memory
b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.scenario: At a Budapest history museum, a visiting student asks you what Heroes' Square, Memento Park and Szabadság tér show about how Hungarians remember the past.
b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.prompt: Tell her what the leaders of the Dualist era decided, and what Budapest's leadership proposed for the old statues.
cues: Say what the leaders of the Dualist era decided
Say what Budapest proposed for the statues
b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.target: A dualista korszak vezetői arra a döntésre jutottak, hogy emlékművet emelnek a Hősök terén. Budapest vezetése pedig azzal a kezdeményezéssel állt elő, hogy a szobrokat ne olvasszák be.
b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.english: The leaders of the Dualist era reached the decision to erect a monument on Heroes' Square. Budapest's leadership, in turn, came forward with the initiative that the statues should not be melted down.
b2-politikairetorika-consolidation.canDo: I can explain how Hungarian monuments (Hősök tere, Szoborpark, Szabadság tér) and street names reflect regimes, collective memory, and memory politics.
